s: Substantive due process protects certain liberties from government interference regardless of the procedures used.
When a law burdens a fundamental right, strict scrutiny applies.
Other liberty interests get rational-basis review.

Washington v. Glucksberg (1997) requires (1) a "careful description" of the asserted right and (2) proof that it is "deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition" and "implicit in the concept of ordered liberty."
Obergefell (2015) described a more evolving, "reasoned judgment" approach for marriage.
Dobbs (2022) reaffirmed Glucksberg's history-and-tradition test as the governing method.
The level of generality matters enormously.
Is the right asserted "the right to die," or "the right to refuse unwanted medical treatment"?
Is it "the right to marry," or "the right to same-sex marriage"?
Compare Michael H. v. Gerald D. (1989), footnote 6 (Scalia, J.): use "the most specific level at which a relevant tradition" exists.
Is it deeply rooted in history and tradition and implicit in ordered liberty?
Or is it within a recognized precedent line (marriage, procreation, family, child-rearing, bodily integrity)?
If fundamental: strict scrutiny, meaning a compelling interest and narrowly tailored means.
Consider equal protection as an alternative route when the law burdens the right unequally.
